## Job Market Paper

#### Who Bears the Burden of Bank Capital Regulation? Buffers, Risk Weights, and the Supply of Credit

<span class="journal-tag">Job Market Paper</span>

::: {.paper-links}
[Download PDF](files/jmp.pdf)
:::

<details>
<summary>Abstract</summary>
Who bears the burden of bank capital regulation? Using a quarterly panel of U.S. banks (1994–2019) and narratively identified capital-requirement shocks, we document a sectoral lending channel: within banks, commercial and industrial lending — which carries the higher regulatory risk weight — contracts significantly more than real estate lending, while consumer and credit-card lending do not respond. The intensity of the contraction is governed by a bank's distance to its regulatory frontier: institutions with thin voluntary capital buffers cut lending most, whereas well-buffered banks absorb historical policy innovations with attenuated credit responses. We rationalise these facts with a heterogeneous macro-banking model in which banks facing funding-market frictions hoard precautionary capital buffers, solved globally with deep-learning methods and estimated by simulated method of moments on the within-bank impulse responses. A permanent one-percentage-point tightening carries a welfare cost of 2.4–2.9% of steady-state credit-market surplus, almost entirely through the contraction in the scale of intermediation; differentiated risk weights determine which sectors and which banks bear the contraction, but contribute little to its aggregate cost. These figures are gross transition costs of tightening — the framework prices the credit contraction, not the offsetting stability benefits of capital — so they measure the incidence and burden of regulation, not its optimal level. The model implies that the muted historical response of well-buffered banks is a latent vulnerability: shocks large enough to erode voluntary buffers trigger sharply non-linear credit contractions.
</details>

::: {.practice}
**In one paragraph:** When regulators raise bank capital requirements, who actually pays the price? Using data on roughly 4,800 U.S. banks over twenty-five years, this paper shows that the burden falls unevenly: business lending — which carries a higher risk weight — contracts about forty percent more than mortgage lending, while consumer credit barely responds, and banks with the thinnest capital buffers cut lending 1.29 times more than the best-capitalised institutions. A heterogeneous macro-banking model, solved with deep-learning methods, quantifies the welfare cost at 2.4–2.9% of credit-market surplus per percentage point of tightening and reveals a hidden vulnerability — the voluntary buffers that insulated most banks historically are a finite resource, and sufficiently large shocks trigger sharply non-linear credit contractions.
:::
